title: Trade-offs arising from Sn additions to the Cu-9Al-10Mn ferromagnetic shape memory alloy
abstract: Abstract The addition of several alloying elements has been tested in Cu-Al-Mn alloys, aiming to obtain the best combination of properties, a common challenge in materials engineering. In this work, effects of Sn additions up to 6 wt.% to a Cu-9Al-10Mn shape memory alloy were evaluated by different characterization techniques after quenching in iced water. On the one hand, it was observed that Sn additions decrease the melting temperatures, the grain size, the temperatures for the martensitic reaction, and the shape memory effect. On the other hand, results also showed that Sn additions increase the corrosion resistance and the ferromagnetic behavior of the alloy. Furthermore, Sn additions result in a monophasic microstructure, constituted by an ordered derivative of the β phase, whose structure is like β 1  and β 3 . Hypothesis for the variation of microhardness, martensite start ( M s ) temperature, and the saturation magnetization were given, considering the atomic properties of the Sn atom. The main trade-off involved in the substitution of Cu by Sn in the Cu-9Al-10Mn-xSn (0 <  x  ≤ 6) quaternary alloys is the improvement of magnetic properties to the detriment of the mechanical ones. Graphical abstract

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Cu-Al-Mn alloys have been currently researched as candidates for high technology applications, such as eco-friendly refrigeration through elastocaloric cooling [ 1 ,  2 ], dampers for mechanical vibrations and noise [ 3 ], low-fatigue [ 4 ] and high-temperature [ 5 ] shape memory alloys (SMAs), and actuators for spacecraft deployable thermal radiators [ 6 ]. Reasons for this are their low cost and high thermal and electrical conductivity, despite the fact that they are prone to intergranular cracking [ 5 ].

The Cu-9wt.%Al alloy (or Cu 81 Al 19 , in atomic composition) is located close to the α|α + γ 1  and α|α + α 2 solvus  lines, in the solubility limit of Al in Cu, where ordering effects of both α (with FCC structure) and β (with BCC structure) phases are observed [ 7 ]. One of the advantages of such composition is that it behaves like a (solid) saturated solution, where small perturbations have pronounced effects in its constitution (namely, in its microstructure). Co additions, for example, suppress the eutectoid reaction (β → α + γ 1 ) in this material [ 8 ], while Ga additions have the opposite effect, favoring the formation of the (α + γ 1 ) microconstituent [ 9 ], similar to the pearlite of steels [ 10 ]. Ni additions, in turn, suppress the α phase ordering [ 9 ], although all alloying elements seem to hamper this phase transition in some extent [ 11 ]. Both effects are related to interactions with the solute, that is, the Al atoms. The addition of Mn to this alloy, substituting Cu, results in interesting effects, such as the widening of the stability field of the β phase [ 12 ]. In addition, it introduces additional steps for the β phase ordering, one of them resulting in the formation of a ferromagnetic phase, named β 3 , through a spinodal decomposition (β → β 1  + β 3 , with A2, D0 3 , and L2 1 Strukturbericht  designations, respectively) [ 13 ]. In general, crescent additions of Mn increase the amount of β 3  phase and decrease the melting temperatures [ 14 ], resulting in a non-ferrous ferromagnetic alloy easy to cast. In addition, the presence of ordering is essential for the occurrence of shape memory effect [ 15 ].

Effects of quaternary additions on the phase equilibria of the Cu-9Al-10Mn alloy have been studied in the last years, such as Gd [ 16 ,  17 ] and Ag [ 18 ,  19 ], as well as quinary, such as Ag and Zr [ 20 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 ]. However, until now, the effects of Sn additions to this alloy remain unknown. It is known that Sn increases the saturation magnetization of the Cu-11Al-10Mn alloy [ 24 ]. Moreover, it was found that Sn additions deteriorate the cold workability and the shape memory effect of the Cu 73 Al 17 Mn 10  alloy, which was attributed to an increase in order of the parent phase [ 25 ]. This work aims to evaluate whether it is possible to find a good compromise between these properties and how they evolve along the enrichment of the alloy with Sn.

sections.heading: Manufacturing and heat treatments
paragraphs: Metals with purity greater than 99.95% were melted in an electric arc furnace made by the laboratory staff, with an argon atmosphere and a copper crucible cooled with running water. Pieces of metal were placed in layers, in increasing order of density, in the cavity of the furnace crucible, to ensure homogenization during melting. The furnace atmosphere was prepared by applying a primary vacuum, enriching the atmosphere with argon until a partial pressure of 0.50 atm was reached, and applying a new primary vacuum. This cycle was performed three times to reduce the amount of atmospheric air still present inside the furnace. Before melting, the interior of the furnace was enriched with argon again. Each alloy was melted five times by passing the electric arc through the pieces of metal located in the internal cavity of the crucible, also with the aim of homogenizing the chemical composition of the alloys produced. The manufactured ingots had a mass of approximately 20 g, a length of 30 mm, a diameter of 10 mm, and an approximately elliptical cross section. The mass loss after melting was verified by comparing the total mass of the pure elements added to the crucible for each alloy with the mass of the respective ingot. Mass losses greater than 3% would result in rejection and disposal of the ingot. All alloys presented mass losses of less than 1%. Phase diagrams and Scheil curves were obtained in the Thermo-Calc software, using the database for copper-based alloys TCCU6, to estimate the melting temperatures of the alloys before carrying out the heat treatments. The ingots were annealed at 800 K for 120 h in a self-made tubular furnace. Samples of the annealed ingots were extracted using a Buehler precision cutter, model Isomet 1000, equipped with a diamond disk and cooled with soluble oil. These samples were extracted from the central region of the ingots. They were heated at 800 K for 1 h in a muffle furnace EDG, model F-3000, before quenching in an iced water bath. To facilitate the identification of the analyzed alloys, they will be nominated by an acronym formed by the Mn and Sn amounts, since all alloys present 9 wt.% Al and the balance of the alloy is composed by Cu. Therefore, 10Mn-0.5Sn corresponds to the Cu-10Mn-9Al-0.5Sn alloy. All compositions reported in this way in the present work are in mass percentage.

sections.heading: Characterization
paragraphs: Optical microscopy (OM) analyses were performed using an Olympus metallurgical microscope, model BX41M-LED. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were acquired by a JEOL electronic microscope, model JSM6610LV, equipped with a Thermo Fisher energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS) detector, model UltraDry. Microhardness measurements were performed on a Shimadzu microhardness tester, model HMV-2 T, with a load of 0.5 kgf (HV0.5) and application of the same for 10 s. Each value reported in this work corresponds to an average of 15 measurements. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) curves were obtained on a TA Instruments equipment, model DSC Q20, equipped with Pt crucibles and on a NETZSCH equipment, model DSC 204 F1 Phoenix, equipped with Al crucibles. Thermomechanical analysis (TMA) curves were obtained on a Linseis equipment, model TMA PT1600, with a sample holder of quartz and a pre-load of 50 mN. DSC analyses were performed with a cooling/heating rate of 10 K min −1  and an argon flux of 50 mL min −1 , while TMA analyses were performed with a cooling/heating rate of 2 K min −1 .

The as-quenched 10Mn-xSn alloys were analyzed by high-energy X-ray diffraction (HEXRD) at the P07 beamline of the (Positron–Electron Tandem Ring Accelerator (PETRA III) of the Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron (DESY) research center. The analysis was performed in transmission mode, with a wavelength of 0.14235 Å and a light beam with an area of 70 μm × 70 μm. The diffracted photons were captured by a PerkinElmer detector. The distance between the sample and the detector was calibrated with lanthanum hexaboride (LaB 6 ). Diffraction patterns were obtained from the transmission figures using the free software General Structure Analysis System (GSAS-II) [ 26 ]. The identification of diffraction peaks was done with the help of the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD) and the free version of the Crystal Impact Diamond software.

Magnetization curves as a function of the temperature (M vs. T) were obtained in a third-generation MPMS SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device) 7.0 Tesla magnetometer with a vibrating-sample magnetometer (VSM) module. The curves were obtained after calibration of the sample position, removal of the remanence at 300 K, and cooling down to 2 K. Curves were obtained in the absence of a magnetic field (zero field cooling, ZFC) and in the presence of a magnetic field equal to 200 Oe (field cooling, FC), in a temperature range between 2 and 400 K. Magnetization curves as a function of the applied magnetic field (M vs. H) were obtained after the M versus T curves at temperatures of 300 and 2 K.

Note: Both martensite start temperature and saturation magnetization are represented by the same symbol in the literature. To avoid any confusion between these terms in the present work, the symbol  M s  will refer solely to the martensite start temperature.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: Figure  1  shows phase diagrams calculated by the Thermo-Calc software for the Cu-9Al-10Mn-xSn (0 <  x  < 10) region. Fig. 1 a  Phase diagram calculated for Cu-9Al-10Mn-xSn (0 <  x  ≤ 6) alloys. Red lines denote compositions analyzed in the present work ( x  = 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 6).  b  Details at smaller temperatures from ( a )

Figure  1 a shows that Sn additions decrease the temperatures for the  liquidus  and (β + L) field lines. From a technological point of view, Sn additions enhance the castability of the 10Mn-xSn alloys in the evaluated region, reducing the energy needed for its melting, but they also result in the need for heat treatments at low temperatures, to avoid the ingot loss inside the furnace. In addition, it is possible to see in Fig.  1 b that the β  transus  line presents a little increase in its temperature around 3.5% Sn. Cooling from this line results in the formation of T 3 -Cu 3 Mn 2 Al, β Mn , and ε-Cu 3 Sn phases, as the Sn content increases. Except for the second phase, these phases are intermetallic compounds. Therefore, quenching from intercritical temperatures will result in microstructures consisting of an ordered derivative of β phase coexisting with at least one of these phases, depending on the Sn amount in the alloy. Such a condition is harmful for SMAs, since these phases do not present shape memory effect and are brittle. However, the phase diagram supposes that melting and solidification occurs at the thermodynamic equilibrium, a condition that, in practice, is very hard to reach. Therefore, there is the possibility that the liquid phase is formed below the previous calculated  liquidus  line. One way to overcome this is through the calculation of solidification curves based on the classic Gulliver–Scheil model [ 15 ,  27 ]. Even though it is still a model, it can give insight into the inferior limit of the melting temperature range.

Figure  2  shows solidification curves based on the Scheil–Gulliver model calculated by the Thermo-Calc software for the 10Mn-0.5Sn and 10Mn-6Sn alloys, extremes of the composition range. Fig. 2 Solidification curves based on the Scheil–Gulliver model calculated by the Thermo-Calc software for the 10Mn-0.5Sn and 10Mn-6Sn alloys

According to Fig.  2 , there is a considerable deviation between the equilibrium and the classic Scheil–Gulliver model, in such a way that, considering this model, the melting temperature start of these alloys decreases from about 1073–848 K. In addition, the model also suggests an increasingly complex melting route as the Sn amount increases in the 10Mn-xSn alloys, denoted by sudden changes in the slope of curves (they represent different steps of the solidification). Therefore, according to Figs.  1  and  2 , 800 K is an effective and safe temperature for the heat treatment of the 10Mn-xSn (0 <  x  < 6) alloys, since no intermetallic or liquid phase is stable at this temperature.

Figure  3  shows OM images from the as-quenched studied alloys. Fig. 3 OM images obtained from as-quenched samples of the studied alloys:  a  10Mn-0.5Sn,  b  10Mn-1Sn, and  c  10Mn-2Sn.  d  10Mn-4Sn.  e  10Mn-6Sn

According to Eq. ( 1 ), Sn-rich alloys and environments with high concentration of dissolved iron (III) cations favor the deposit of metallic iron in the surface. Since the standard potential for the above reaction is positive (E° > 0), it is spontaneous and happens during the etching of the 10Mn-4Sn and 10Mn-6Sn alloys with ferric chloride solutions. Other etchants were employed (based on ammonium persulfate, ammonium hydroxide, and nitric acid [ 29 ]), but without success. This result suggests that the increase in Sn amount (≥ 4%) results in the increment of the corrosion resistance of the Cu-9Al-10Mn-xSn alloys.

It is also possible to see in Fig.  3  that, in general, crescent Sn additions reduce grain size, although grains from the 10Mn-4Sn alloy seem larger than those from the 10Mn-2Sn alloy. On the other hand, the reduction in the grain size is expressive in the 10Mn-6Sn alloy, since a higher magnification was needed to observe the etched grain boundaries. It is important to say that grains are tridimensional, multifaceted, and present a complex shape, in such a way that measurements performed on one of the grain surfaces can differ from those made in others [ 30 ], which explains why measurements for the estimation of the average grain diameter are performed in several directions of the sample [ 31 ]. Therefore, images from Fig.  3  just allow to see the effect of Sn in the grain growth in one direction.

It is well known that alloying elements tend to be segregated to grain boundaries of the parent phase to decrease the strain imposed on its crystalline lattice. In addition, it is also known that these solute atoms hind the movement of grain boundaries, inhibiting grain growth [ 30 ]. Therefore, higher times of heating will be needed for the grain growth in an alloyed austenite in comparison with another one without solute atoms. In this case, eventual effects arising from the presence of Mn are being ignored, since all alloys were produced with the same amount of this element. Since all alloys were heated up before quenching for the same time (1 h), but present different amounts of Sn (0 <  x  ≤ 6% Sn), this difference was already expected.

Figure  4  shows a SEM image from the microstructure of an as-quenched sample of the 10Mn-6Sn alloy (namely, the studied alloy with the higher amount of Sn) with a linear EDXS analysis. Fig. 4 SEM image from the microstructure of an as-quenched sample of the 10Mn-6Sn alloy with a linear EDXS analysis

It is possible to see on Fig.  4  that there is no preferential location for the elements that compose the studied materials, even at 6% Sn, in such a way that they form a substitutional solid solution. Therefore, it is expected that these materials present a monophasic microstructure and higher magnifications do not obtain additional information.

Figure  5  shows the austenite microhardness as a function of the Sn amount in the studied alloys and graphs that illustrate two hypotheses to explain the observed variation. They will be discussed in the next sections. Fig. 5 a  Austenite microhardness as a function of the Sn amount of the studied alloys.  b – d  Details from Fig. 5a showing possible laws for the variation in the austenite microhardness

The mean value of microhardness from the as-quenched Cu-9Al-10Mn alloy (without Sn) was measured for comparison in Fig.  5 a. In general, it is possible to observe that the Sn additions increase the microhardness of austenite. However, there are two distinctive behaviors regarding the variation in this mechanical property: one up to 2% Sn, detailed in Fig.  5 b, and other between 2 and 6% Sn, detailed in Fig.  5 c. These behaviors are related to the occurrence and predominance of different phenomena.

Up to 2% Sn, the Vickers microhardness from the 10Mn-xSn alloys present a parabolic dependence of the Sn amount (Fig.  5 b). This type of relationship was observed in the mechanical properties from other systems, such as the flow strength of high purity Al-Mg alloys due to solid solution strengthening (SSS) [ 32 ]. At the beginning of alloying, solute atoms significantly distort the crystalline lattice of the unit cells from the host phase. With this distortion, the alloyed unit cells become incoherent with the unalloyed ones, which will hinder dislocation movement [ 33 ]. However, at a certain point, depending on the metallurgical system, most of the unit cells is already distorted, in such a way that the distortion of additional unit cells will result, on the contrary, in an increase in coherence. Since a decrease in microhardness was observed at the small Sn amount of 2% in the 10Mn-xSn alloys, it is reasonable to assume that this atom prefers a specific atomic site from the austenite, which is less available than the others, and that Sn atoms efficiently distort the austenite. It is known that ordered austenitic phases (β 2 , β 1 , and β 3 ) from high Mn Cu-Al-Mn alloys present a body-centered cubic (BCC) unit cell, where Al and Mn atoms tend to occupy the central site [ 34 ]. Therefore, Sn atoms, which are 23% larger than Al atoms [ 35 ], probably occupy central sites from some of the unit cells of the ordered austenite, and at 2% Sn, some coherence between the distorted unit cells takes place.

From 2 to 6% Sn (Fig.  5 c), the austenitic phase microhardness from the 10Mn-xSn alloys seems to present a linear relation with the Sn amount. This behavior resembles the Hall–Petch effect (HPE), present in polycrystalline metals. Dislocations moving from one grain to another must change their orientation when crossing a grain boundary, and the difficulty to change this orientation increases with the angle of the common grain boundary. The increase in the total grain boundary surface (and, therefore, the reduction in the grain size) results in a greater chance of these episodes of dislocation movement prevention happen during the material deformation [ 33 ]. In fact, a finer granulometry was observed in Fig.  3 e for the 10Mn-6Sn alloy in comparison with that from the 10Mn-2Sn alloy, as well as a higher Vickers microhardness value in Fig.  5 a.

However, a question that arises from Fig.  5 a is related to the extension of this phenomenon predominance in each case. Is it reasonable to assume, for simplification, that they occur separately or is it possible (and more accurate) to consider that they occur simultaneously? To answer this question and explain the observed behavior from the as-quenched 10Mn-Sn alloys, two hypotheses were given.

H1 has two problems. First, the number of unit cells is infinitely higher than the total grain boundaries surface. Therefore, there are still more available atomic sites in the austenite cell units to be occupied by Sn atoms than in the vicinity of the grain boundaries, so a change in the composition of austenite is expected from Sn amounts above 2 wt.%. Second, the segregation of Sn at the grain boundaries would result in the formation of a second phase at higher temperature that would be retained after the quenching, which was not observed in the Thermo-Calc simulations (Fig.  1 ) neither in the OM images (Fig.  3 ) for the studied compositions. Thus, although Eqs. ( 2 ) and ( 3 ) fit the obtained data, it is not believed that HPE predominance will occur indefinitely until the formation of a new phase.

The second hypothesis (H2) consists in the assumption that the 10Mn-xSn alloys present multiple steps of SSS and crystalline coherence increase due to the alloying of several unit cells (resulting in a microhardness decrease), followed again by SSS and grain size reduction (resulting in a microhardness increase). In H2, the contribution of SSS in the new increase in hardness is not neglected, because there is the possibility that Sn atoms occupy other atomic sites from the already distorted unit cell. When it happens, there is crystalline coherence loss, since there are close unit cells distorted with different amounts of Sn atoms, as well as undistorted ones.

The plot of  I h  (% Sn) in Fig.  5 d shows a different situation of H1. Instead of resulting in a maximum of hardness in the analyzed series of alloys, according to Fig.  5 d and the discussion made before, the addition of 6 wt.% Sn can result in an increase in crystalline coherence and, therefore, in a reduction of hardness. If H2 is correct, the theoretical alloy 10Mn-5Sn (which was not studied in this work) will present a higher Vickers microhardness value in comparison with the other investigated alloys. This verification must be done in the future. In addition, since the I h  curve was obtained by interpolation (namely, it is a curve that passes through the experimental data), the coefficient of determination is equal to the unity. Details from the fitting of curves in Fig.  5 b–d can be found in Fig.  1 S– 3 S of the Supplementary Material. An obvious consequence of using this function to describe the variation of the mechanical properties of an alloy is that the greater the number of quaternary additions, the greater the degree of the polynomial must be to know the effects of such additions. Since the function is a fifth-degree polynomial which ends in the microhardness value of the 10Mn-6Sn alloy, the degree of I n  (n) is equal to  x− 1, being  x  the amount of Sn and, consequently, a natural number. Finally, it is important to highlight that the analyzed materials present BCC structures. Therefore, other behaviors may be expected due to alloying in materials with different crystalline structures.

The possibility of describing microhardness evolution with alloying by a known function that considers both SSS and HPE can be useful for the following reasons: First, it will allow a better estimation of other mechanical properties due to the correlation between microhardness and them [ 33 ,  36 ], resulting in a lesser need for other more expensive mechanical tests (obviously, if this relationship is proven with greater robustness and considering the absence of discontinuities in the analyzed material). Second, if the variation of the polynomial coefficients with composition (for example, how they change if Sn is substituted by other quaternary additions) and heat treatment parameters (such as time, temperature, and quenching media) is known, effects of manufacturing and processing on the mechanical properties may be foreseen before tests and fabrication, resulting in raw materials, energy, and time saving during alloy design. Third, it will allow that formulations that result in ductile SMAs to be predicted, which will be less prone to damage during rolling and drawing operations, as well as in application, a well-known drawback for Cu-based SMAs [ 37 ,  38 – 39 ].

From this point, it is important to emphasize that this attempt to describe the mechanical behavior of the Cu-9Al-10Mn-xSn alloys is still a hypothesis due to experimental limitations. A proper investigation of the HPE contribution for the microhardness evolution (and possibly other mechanical properties) would demand mean grain size measurements, which are not possible on these materials due to the difficulty to etch their grain boundaries properly for high Sn amounts. In addition, less alloyed samples present larger grains, in such a way that few grains are present in the ingots. Consequently, several ingots are needed to have a representative mean grain size: According to the technical standard ASTM E112, it would be achieved by the measurement of 50–100 grains [ 31 ]. Since the grains are large, multiple fields of the same sample and slices of the same ingot will measure almost always the same grains. Therefore, large grain size for low Sn amounts and poor grain boundary etching for concentrated alloys are the main limitations for a better evaluation of the influence of HPE on microhardness. Finally, since it is not possible to properly reveal grain boundaries in alloys from the upper Sn limit, it is also hard to evaluate the single contribution of SSS to microhardness (Does the indentation touch the surface of a single grain or not?).

Figure  6  shows HEXRD patterns obtained from as-quenched samples of the studied alloys and compares the difference between the observed 2θ values with the theoretical 2θ values from two phases, β 1  (with Cu 3 Al stoichiometry) and β 3  (with Cu 2 MnAl stoichiometry). Fig. 6 a – e  Details from the HEXRD patterns obtained from as-quenched samples of the studied alloys.  f  δ 2θ  values in relation to the theoretical 2θ values of the β 1  and β 3  phases, computed for the most intense peaks on Fig. 6a–e

It is possible to note in the full HEXRD spectra of the 10Mn-xSn alloys (see Fig.  4 S of the  Supplementary Material ), the presence of one to two diffraction peaks in the HEXRD patterns obtained, which are considerably more intense than the noise in the baseline. One can observe in Fig.  6 a–e that the 2θ values from these peaks decrease as the Sn amount increases. Considering the Bragg’s law [ 33 ], this is evidence that the interplanar distance in the austenitic phase is increasing with alloying. The substitution of Cu atoms by Sn atoms possibly results in the introduction of compressive stresses in the crystalline lattice of the austenite that dilate this phase. According to Fig.  6 f, the increase in the Sn amount results in a phase less similar to β 1  and more similar to β 3 . It is worth mentioning that there is no Crystallographic Information File (CIF) for this unprecedented Sn-alloyed austenite [ 40 ]. As stated before, these phases differ in the occupation of the central atomic site by Mn instead of Al. In the 10Mn-xSn alloys, as suggested during the evaluation of the Vickers microhardness results, some of these sites are probably occupied by Sn atoms, emulating the addition of Mn to β 1 . Considering the huge intensity difference between the diffraction peaks from the austenitic phase and the noises in the baseline, as well as the fact that they occur at 2θ values that do not match with values from other possible phases and oxides, it is believed that they are solely due to background radiation. The presence of diffraction peaks related to the presence of just one phase is in accordance with the Thermo-Calc simulations and the OM images, which describe a single-phase microstructure stable at higher temperature which was retained after quenching.

A priori, one could perform a Rietveld refinement of the HEXRD spectra from Fig.  6 , refining the position of the atomic sites to evaluate the probability of the occupation of each atomic site of the unit cell by the Sn atom, thus having an idea of the crystalline structure. However, it is important to stress that Rietveld refining is more appropriate for powdered materials. Bulk materials present preferred orientation that leads to incorrect intensities measurements (namely, the model presents diffraction peaks with significant intensity difference when compared to the experimental data). This feature cannot be removed, for example, with sample rotation [ 41 ]. Preferred orientation can also affect the thermal parameters related to atom vibration inside the phase lattice [ 42 ]. Powdering of a metastable material such as this austenite before XRD also results in another problem: The energy employed for scratch, sand, grind, or crush the sample can be enough to transform this phase (for example, some or solely martensite can be observed after these powdering operations due to mechanically induced transformation of the austenite) [ 15 ].

Although transmission electron microscopy (TEM) can be a powerful alternative, it can also lead to several artifacts and misinterpretations [ 43 ], as well as the formation of new phases due to beam-induced atomic displacements (knock-on effect), which was observed in certain systems [ 44 ,  45 ,  46 ,  47 – 48 ]. Due to these risks and the complexity of the sample preparation inherent to TEM [ 49 ], a faster and qualitative approach with HEXRD was chosen. However, the authors recognize the usefulness of a future investigation of the alloyed austenite structure with TEM, since under carefully controlled beam energy. Once it is known that the microstructure is monophasic, the identification of new phases under TEM can be considered as an artifact.

Effects of alloying elements on the mechanical properties of shape memory alloys, such as hardness, cold workability, and those obtained under tensile stresses, as well as the shape memory effect itself, are of main interest for the application of these materials in new devices. However, during alloying, changes in the atoms from a solid solution, such as austenite, can result not only in strains of the crystalline lattice and changes in the chemical interactions between solvent and solute atoms, but also in changes in the magnetic ones, resulting from vectorial summations of the electronic magnetic moments. Therefore, it is desirable to know how these magnetic interactions inside the ferromagnetic parent phase are affected by increasing amounts of a new element.

Figure  7  shows M versus T curves obtained from as-quenched samples of the studied alloys. Fig. 7 M versus T curves obtained from as-quenched samples of the studied alloys during the ZFC–FC cycle:  a  10Mn-0.5Sn,  b  10Mn-1Sn,  c  10Mn-2Sn,  d  10Mn-4Sn,  e  10Mn-6Sn alloy

It is possible to observe in Fig.  7 a–b the presence of two events that occur during heating (ZFC subcurve), one between 2 and 125 K and the other between 125 and 200 K. It is also noted that the event that occurs at lower temperatures is more intense in the 10Mn-0.5Sn alloy and less intense in the 10Mn-1Sn alloy. The identification of these two events during heating is lost in the curves of Fig.  7 c–e, so that only one large event is observed between 2 and 200 K. These results suggest that the increase in the Sn content causes these events to occur in much closer temperature intervals, in such a way that they overlap.

The first event, which occurs at lower temperatures in the alloys with 0.5 wt.% Sn and 1 wt.% Sn, and which possibly also occurs in the other studied alloys, has already been observed in ZFC–FC curves of other alloys derived from the Cu-Al-Mn system [ 50 ,  51 ,  52 ,  53 – 54 ]. As in [ 54 ], such curves undergo a bifurcation at temperatures close to 25 K, in such a way that the heating curve (after cooling at zero field, ZFC) is different from the cooling curve (under a field of 200 Oe, FC), and are related to different phenomena. The increase in the magnetic moment in the ZFC curves is attributed to the thawing of ferromagnetic clusters that were randomly frozen in various metastable states. On the other hand, the decrease in the magnetic moment in the FC curves is related to antiferromagnetic interactions between these clusters [ 54 ], which probably occur due to the presence of the magnetic field. The application of the magnetic field promotes reorientation of the magnetic domains, which become antiparallel to each other, resulting in the previously cited antiferromagnetic interactions.

Trehern evaluated the actuation ability at cryogenic temperatures (< 123 K) in Cu-Al-Mn alloys with nominal Al contents around 19 at.% and Mn between 11.97 at.% and 12.77 at.% [ 55 ], composition ranges very close to those of the alloys studied in this work, but without the additions of Sn. The temperatures for the reversible martensitic transformation in these materials, needed for the actuation at cryogenic temperatures, ranged from 150 K ≥  M s  ≥ 70 K and from 120 K ≥  M f  ≥ 47 K [ 55 ]. Therefore, it is possible that the second event (observed in Fig.  7 a and b at higher temperatures) is related to the formation of a martensitic phase with a ferromagnetic character more pronounced than the austenite and that the additions of Sn further reduced the temperatures for their occurrence (which would explain the formation of the bands observed in Fig.  7 c, d, and e). As observed in the literature for other metallurgical systems [ 15 ], there is an increase in the magnetic moment associated with the martensitic transformation in the 10Mn-xSn alloys. Apparently, the presence of a magnetic field “suppresses” the martensitic transformation in the 10Mn-1Sn and 10Mn-0.5Sn alloys (Fig.  7 a and b, respectively).

Finally, it is noted that the peak associated with the reversible martensitic transformation (β 1 ′ → β 1  in the ZFC curve, β 1  → β 1 ′ in the FC curve) changes with the increase in the Sn content. In the ZFC curves, its intensity increases up to 2 wt.% Sn. In the FC curves, this peak is not observed in the alloy with 0.5 wt.% Sn but reappears in the alloy with 1 wt.% Sn. The bands observed in the other M versus T curves due to the overlap of the magnetic events described above are visible in both the ZFC and FC curves, indicating that the increase in the Sn content prevents the “suppression” of the martensitic transformation in the presence of a magnetic field in the analyzed temperature range. However, this is not a suppression indeed.

It is known that the application of a magnetic field increases the difference in the Gibbs energy between the austenite and martensite; that is, it increases the magnitude of the driving force required for the martensitic transformation to occur. One consequence of this increase in the Gibbs energy is an increase in the  M s  temperature [ 15 ]. This effect can be explained in terms of entropy variation. The application of a magnetic field to the austenite reorganizes its crystal structure, removing part of the disorder present in the austenite that was stable at high temperatures into the furnace, decreasing its entropy and increasing its Gibbs energy and, consequently, the  M s  temperature. Therefore, the apparent “suppression” of the martensitic transformation observed in Fig.  7 a–b is, in fact, a shifting of this same phase transformation to temperatures higher than those of the analysis. For this reason, the effect is more pronounced in the 10Mn-0.5Sn and 10Mn-1Sn alloys. Since their parent phases are less deformed by the presence of Sn atoms in the crystal structure, only minor stimuli are required to reorganize the system. This leads to a decrease in entropy, an increase in Gibbs free energy, and consequently a rise in the temperature at which the martensitic transformation occurs.

Figure  8  shows M versus H curves obtained from as-quenched samples of the studied alloys. Fig. 8 M versus H curves from as-quenched samples of the studied alloys, obtained at different temperatures:  a  300 K and  b  2 K

It is possible to observe in Fig.  8  that the saturation magnetization is proportional to the Sn content of the 10Mn-xSn alloys, both at 300 K and 2 K, although the values are higher at 2 K (approximately twice those observed at 300 K). It happens because the spin waves excitations (or magnons) of electrons at this temperature are practically zero, thus preventing the cancelation of interactions between their respective spins, as well because the martensitic structure (stable at 2 K) provides more favorable interactions than the austenitic structure (stable at 300 K). It is noted that, at 2 K, the curves of the 10Mn-2Sn and 10Mn-4Sn alloys overlap, presenting very similar behaviors, although it is still possible to increase the saturation magnetization when the Sn content is increased to 6%. From these results, it is possible to conclude that the presence of Sn atoms in the austenitic and martensitic phases intensifies their ferromagnetic character, which is more pronounced in the martensite.

The ferromagnetic character presented by some Cu-Al-Mn alloys is attributed to Ruderman–Kittel–Kasuya–Yosida (RKKY) interactions [ 13 ]. In this kind of interaction, there is an exchange coupling between a magnetic ion in a metal crystal and its conduction electrons, which polarize the electrons in the vicinity of this ion. It results in an indirect exchange interaction between this magnetic ion and a second one, because this second ion perceives the magnetization induced by the first one through the conduction electrons [ 56 ]. Consequently, it is believed that the substitution of Cu by Sn in the 10Mn-xSn alloys enhances the RKKY interactions, because there is an increase in the total amount of conduction electrons, since metals present an overlapping of the valence and conduction bands [ 33 ], and an atom with one electron in the last electronic shell is replaced by another with four. In other words, the “medium” for indirect exchange interactions becomes “more conductive.”

The influence of Mn and Sn additions on the thermomagnetic behavior of the Cu-Al-Mn alloys becomes remarkable when results from Fig.  8 a are compared to those from a recent work, which investigated steps for magnetic ordering and their temperature range in ternary CuAlMn alloys with 25 at.% Al (therefore, with a higher amount of this element compared to that of the present work, around 19 at.%) and Mn ranging from 6 to 8 at.% (while the alloys studied here have this element ranging from 10.2 to 10.4 at.%), along a region delimited by the Cu 3 Al (pure β 1 ) and Cu 2 MnAl (pure β 3 ) compositions [ 57 ]. Results from [ 57 ] are comparable to Fig.  8 a due to the similarity in the employed experimental procedure (arc-melted and then as-quenched alloys in iced water, as well as M vs. H measurements at room temperature), a feature hard to find in the literature for the evaluation of other properties.

While as-quenched alloys from [ 57 ] presented paramagnetic behavior, as-quenched Cu-9Al-10Mn-xSn alloys presented a ferromagnetic behavior even in this condition. Furthermore, the as-quenched Cu-9Al-10Mn-2Sn alloy showed a saturation magnetization larger than those presented by slowly cooled alloys from [ 57 ], a more favorable condition for magnetic ordering. Therefore, proper alloy formulations can even surpass changes resulting from heat treatment, which reinforces the need for a best comprehension of alloying-induced effects on magnetic properties. However, it is important to highlight that objectives from both works are very different and not devoted to obtaining “the best Heusler alloy,” in such a way that these comparisons are made in a very respectful way.

Figure  9  shows some DSC curves obtained at low temperature for the 10Mn-xSn ( x  = 0.5, 1, or 2%) alloys. Table  2  shows the temperatures for the thermoelastic martensitic transformation (TMT) obtained by the DSC curves from the Fig.  9 a–c. DSC curves from Fig.  9 a–c were obtained in equipment with a lower temperature range of operation to measure the transformation temperatures. DSC curves from Fig.  9 d–f were obtained in equipment with smaller pans, which results in a better resolution of the thermal events. Fig. 9 a – c  DSC curves obtained at low temperature from as-quenched samples of the studied alloys. 10Mn-4Sn and 10Mn-6Sn alloys were not analyzed because the presented transformation temperatures are below the operation limit of the equipment.  d – f  DSC curves from the 10Mn-0.5Sn alloy in different conditions, obtained with different equipment Table 2 Temperatures for the TMT obtained by the DSC curves from Fig.  9 a–c Alloy M s  (K) M f  (K) A s  (K) A f  (K) 10Mn-0.5Sn 265 243 226 251 10Mn-1Sn 245 218 198 231 10Mn-2Sn 190 173 153 168

In the DSC curves in Fig.  9 , it is possible to observe the occurrence of an exothermic event during cooling and an endothermic event during the heating of the studied alloys. These events correspond, respectively, to the austenite–martensite and martensite–austenite transitions [ 12 ]. It can be seen in Fig.  9 a–c and Table  2  that the increase in the Sn content reduces the temperature range in which these transitions occur, so that the analysis could not be performed in the 10Mn-4Sn and 10Mn-6Sn alloys.

Figure  9 d–f shows DSC curves obtained for the 10Mn-0.5Sn alloy (the alloy with the higher temperature range for the martensitic transformation among the 10Mn-xSn alloys) after quenching (Fig.  9 d) and aging at 473 K for 15 (Fig.  9 e) and 30 min (Fig.  9 f). The effects of aging on temperatures and the transformation range (described in Cu-Al-Mn alloys before by Kainuma [ 58 ] and Sutou [ 25 ]) are evident: After tempering, the transformation begins around 215 K and ends at temperatures below the equipment operating temperatures, while after aging, this temperature increases to around 265 K. However, this effect is limited to around 100 K [ 58 ], so that, even after aging, the 10Mn-0.5Sn alloy does not present a temperature range for the martensitic transformation higher than the room temperature (298 K). Increasing the aging time only makes the martensitic transformation smoother, decreasing the intensity of the jerky steps characteristic of the TMT that occurs in some Cu-Al alloys, in which the interfaces of the product phase (martensite) move suddenly in relation to the parent phase (austenite), which manifests itself in the DSC curve as a noisy signal [ 59 ]. Another effect conferred by aging is to reduce the temperature range in which the transformation occurs, shifting this range to higher temperatures and making it narrower. Regarding SMAs, low times and temperatures of aging are preferred, because aging can decrease the shape recovery in Cu-Al-Mn alloys [ 58 ] and lead to the bainitic precipitation, which can decrease the transformation temperatures and fragilize the SMA [ 60 ].

On the other hand, the apparent proportionality between the reduction in transformation temperatures (Fig.  9 ) and the variation in the 2θ values of the austenitic phase with increasing Sn content (Fig.  6 ) suggests a potential correlation, which may contribute to the development of a hypothesis regarding the martensitic transformation in the presence of alloying elements.

Figure  10  shows some TMA curves obtained at low temperatures for the 10Mn-xSn alloys ( x  = 0.5; 1; 2) and after a compressive strain equal to 10% of the alloy length. Fig. 10 TMA curves obtained at low temperature from  a – c  as-quenched samples of the studied alloys and  d  after a compressive strain (10% of the sample length)

In Fig.  10 a–c, one can observe that the 10Mn-xSn ( x  = 0.5; 1; 2) alloys present very different TMA curves. The curve from the 10Mn-1Sn alloy exhibits a higher displacement during the TMT, when compared to the TMA curve from the 10Mn-0.5Sn alloy, while no TMT was detected in the TMA curve from the 10Mn-2Sn alloy, possibly because it occurs below the equipment operating temperature. Furthermore, the TMA curves from Fig.  10 a–c display transformation temperatures different from that shown by Table  2 , acquired from the DSC curves in Fig.  9 a, c. In general, the  M s  and  M f  temperatures in DSC are higher, while the  A s  and  A f  temperatures in DSC are lower than in TMA. Considering that, in TMA, the increase in Sn from 0.5 to 1% decreased the  M s  temperature in 20 K and the  M f  in 40 K, a  M s  temperature around 200 K and a  M f  temperature around 120 K were expected in TMA for the 10Mn-2Sn alloy, supposing a linear dependence of these temperatures with the composition. Indeed, a change in the baseline is observed around 225 K for the TMA curve of the 10Mn-2Sn alloy (red circle in Fig.  10 ). The TMT possibly demands smaller cooling rates (below 2 K min −1 ) to be observed in this material, but in a temperature range very close to the operation limit of the equipment (around 125 K).

Differences in the measured transformation temperatures can be attributed to two reasons. First, DSC detects released or absorbed heat, while TMA detects dimensional changes. Therefore, they detect different phenomena that can occur at different levels of energy. Second, TMA samples are larger than DSC samples, in such a way that they need to be subjected to lower temperatures to exhibit expansion during the martensitic transformation and to higher temperatures to exhibit compression during the inverse transition to austenite. The same happens even if two DSC samples of the same material but with different masses are heated—the sample with the largest mass will present higher transition temperatures during heating [ 62 ].

Figure  10 d shows the TMA curves from the as-quenched 10Mn-0.5Sn and 10Mn-1Sn alloys obtained after a compressive strain that corresponds to 10% of the sample length, to evaluate the shape memory effect. While the 10Mn-0.5Sn alloy presented a shape recovery of 2.6% (26% of the total strain), the 10Mn-1Sn alloy presented a shape recovery equal to 0.4% (4% of the total strain). The other alloys studied did not exhibit any evidence of shape recovery.

A common issue that arises when comparing strain recovery data from shape memory alloys is that there is no standardized way to measure this property, so the results are often obtained through different methods (TMA, DSC, tensile, compression, bending, resistivity measurements, etc.) and conditions (type of microstructure, applied strain, alloy manufacturing method, etc.). It becomes clear in the review done by Mazzer, where several results of strain recovery were presented along with their respective methodologies [ 39 ]. For example, in the present work, a strain of 10% of the sample length was employed. Some works found in this review [ 39 ] used other strain values, such as 6.5 [ 63 ], 5 [ 64 ], and 2% [ 65 ]. In these works, a strain recovery higher than 75% was obtained, although the other previously cited variables may have interfered with the results [ 63 ,  64 – 65 ], which limits performance comparisons. The issue persists even when these comparisons are restricted to Cu-Al-Mn alloys and their derivatives, where other variables beyond composition are present, as found in recent works [ 66 ,  67 ,  68 – 69 ]. It reflects the current situation of these materials.

Although there are some standards for SME evaluation in Ni-Ti alloys, such as ASTM F2082 (“Standard Test Method for Determination of Transformation Temperature of Nickel-Titanium Shape Memory Alloys by Bend and Free Recovery”), sometimes they cannot be employed in Cu-based ones, since they are devoted to products or semifinished parts. For example, the previously mentioned standard describes a test method for wires, tubes, and strip samples. One of the main drawbacks for Cu-based SMAs is precisely to reach enough ductility levels that allow mechanical forming operations, such as drawing, extrusion, and rolling. Therefore, these materials are a “step back” regarding application, and it also includes mechanical properties evaluation before further processing and use. Moreover, the lack of common procedures for mechanical properties evaluation of Cu-based SMAs can be related to a possible need for adequation of the experiment to (new) materials. If severe parameters are used, such as high pre-strain values before testing or high area reduction values during conformation, risk of failure and loss of the sample become significant, making research on the theme more expensive, and a test condition suitable for one alloy may not be the most appropriate for another.

Sutou evaluated the shape memory effect in a Cu 73 Al 17 Mn 10  alloy and after quaternary additions up to 2 at.% and found that Ti, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Au, and Zn improved this property, in contrast to Ag, Si, and Sn (the same element studied in the present work). As stated before, the harmful effect of Sn was attributed to an increase in the degree of order of the ternary alloy, which is similar to the addition of more Al [ 25 ]. However, the obtained results can give insights regarding the improvement of the shape memory effect of Cu-based alloys through alloying.

What drives the attention in the results obtained by Sutou (they will be discussed in the next paragraphs) is the fact that Ti, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, and Zn are all transition metals from the fourth period of the periodic table, the same period of Cu [ 70 ], the balance element of the analyzed alloys. It suggests that low differences in the electronegativity and atomic radius values, as well as similarity in the electronic structures (no presence of p electrons in the last electronic shell, like in the elements Si and Sn), when compared to the Cu atom are requirements for a quaternary addition result in a fair shape recovery.

Au is the great exception here, since it is two periods below Cu. However, this element is from the same family of Cu and Ag and, in contrast to Ag, presents a great solubility in Cu: Continuous solid solution is expected for the Cu-Au system at high temperatures, with the formation of metastable ordered solid solutions only in the Au-rich region, depending on the cooling rate, while Cu and Ag form an eutectic system composed of two solid solutions, with some solid solution formation at higher temperatures [ 71 ]. It is also known that Ag has a great affinity for Al, competing even with Cu to form a BCC phase [ 72 ]. Therefore, solubility in Cu (which is better evaluated by phase diagrams) seems to have a key role in the enhancement of the shape memory effect.

Considering that shape recovery lies in the non-diffusive, coordinated, and short motion of several atoms for the formation of a high symmetry phase [ 15 ], anything that hinders this collective motion will hamper the transformation of martensite in the parent phase. An increase in order can be interpreted as a higher probability of an atomic site in a crystalline lattice to be occupied by a certain atom. If an element tends to “stay” in that atomic site, even short motions will be restrained. In the case of Si and Sn, it can be related to the nature of the chemical bonds formed, since they are in the p block of the periodic table.

In fact, while chemical bonds with a more pronounced ionic character tend to be formed between elements from the extremes of the periodic table (such as halogens and alkaline metals), covalent bonds tend to be formed between elements from this block (like that formed between C and Si and between Ga and As). While in metallic bonds, the electrons are delocalized (like in a Cu-Ni alloy, made of neighbor transition metals), in bonds with a more pronounced covalent character, they tend to be shared only between two elements. Possibly the coordinated movement of atoms is prevented because some of them do not present enough electronic mobility around them to ensure the electrical neutrality (and, therefore, the cohesion and the stability of the metallic lattice) during the shape recovery. These “islands of covalency” are probably located in the Al-Sn and Al-Si pairs inside the parent phase, since Al is also an element from the p block (and, therefore, also has some tendency to form covalent bonds). The increase in the population of these “islands” with the increase in Sn can explain the suppression of the shape memory effect in the 10Mn-xSn alloys.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Results of this work showed that an intensification of the ferromagnetic behavior of the Cu-9Al-10Mn alloy through Sn additions is accompanied by an extenuation of the shape memory effect. The following results were obtained, and hypothesis was developed to explain them: At room temperature, saturation magnetization increases from ~ 5 (10Mn-0.5Sn alloy) to ~ 15 emu.g −1  (10Mn-6Sn alloy) and mild ferromagnetic behavior persists even after quenching. The increase in saturation magnetization by alloying was attributed to an enhancement of the indirect exchange interactions between the ions of the parent phase due to a higher electronic content around them. After a 10% strain, shape recovery decreased from 26% (10Mn-0.5Sn alloy) to 4% (10Mn-1Sn alloy) and was not detected in the other studied alloys. The suppression of the shape memory recovery by alloying was related to the modification of the nature of the chemical bonds formed in the crystalline lattice, which hinders the coordinated movement of atoms during heating for the formation of the parent phase. δ 2θ  values between the parent phase and the β 3  phase decrease from 1.5 to 0.25%. After quenching, Sn additions result in a phase whose crystalline structure possibly lies between β 1  and β 3  phases, in such a way that the addition of Sn to the parent phase seems to emulate the addition of more Mn, expanding the unit cell. The microhardness (and possibly other mechanical properties) change with alloying can be described by a polynomial function (the hardness increment function,  I h ) that considers both SSS and HPE, whose degree ( n ) increases with the Sn amount ( x ), according to the relation  n  =  x− 1.  I h  ranges from 33.6 (0.5% Sn) to 112.2 HV (6% Sn). M s  decreased from 265 (10Mn-0.5Sn alloy) to 190 K (10Mn-2Sn alloy). The TMT for higher Sn amounts is possibly below the working temperature of the equipment used for its detection. The decrease in the  M s  temperature after alloying was explained in terms of an increment of the strain energy needed to start the phase transition. The strain caused by the solid solution possibly needs to be compensated before the martensitic reaction starts.

Additional experimental proof and further improvement of the hypotheses given in the present work are desirable. Possible effects resulting from changes of atomic properties must be verified in the future in other Cu-9Al-10Mn-x alloys. They can lead to a better understanding of how alloying changes properties of the cheap and easy to make Cu-based shape memory alloys, resulting in better formulations and, consequently, in an expansion of their commercial appeal, manufacturing and use, as well as in raw materials saving.
